elements.text: Wettability of Poly(styrene-co-acrylate) Ionomers Improved by Oxygen-Plasma Source Ion Implantation
HYUNEUI LIM,<sup>1</sup> YEONHEE LEE,<sup>1</sup> SEUNGHEE HAN,<sup>1</sup> YOUNGWOO KIM,<sup>1</sup> JU-MYUNG SONG,<sup>2</sup> JOON-SEOP KIM<sup>2</sup>
<sup>1</sup> Advanced Analysis Center, Korea Institute of Science and Technology, #39-1, Haweolgok dong, Seongbuk Gu, Seoul 136-791, Korea
<sup>2</sup> Department of Polymer Science and Engineering, Chosun University, Gwangju 501-600, Korea
Received 5 November 2002; revised 21 April 2003; accepted 23 April 2003

ABSTRACT: The surfaces of poly(styrene-co-acrylic acid) copolymers and their Na- and Cs-neutralized ionomers were modified by O -plasma source ion implantation (PSII) treatment to improve the surface wettability. The changes in the surface wettability, composition, and structure upon the PSII treatment were examined with contact-angle measurements and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy. The untreated surfaces of the acid copolymers and ionomers exhibited different surface energies; this implied clearly that the type of ion species affects the surface hydrophilicity. Also, the PSII treatment induced oxygen-containing groups to reside on the surface and ionic groups to come out toward the surface; this made the surfaces of the ionomers more hydrophilic as compared with that of the acid copolymers. The ionomers also showed slow hydrophobic recovery. Thus, it was suggested that the reduced mobility ofthe polymer chain because of the presence of ionic aggregates results in restricted reorientation of oxygen-containing groups. © 2003 Wiley Periodicals, Inc. J Polym Sci Part B: Polym Phys 41: 1791–1797, 2003 Keywords: ionomers; cold plasma; modification; hydrophilic polymers; ESCA/XPS
INTRODUCTION

Ionomers are ion-containing polymers that have a small number of ionic groups along the nonionic backbone chains. It is widely accepted<sup>1</sup> that the ionic groups in ionomers form aggregates, called multiplets. The presence ofionic aggregates in the ionomers is the most characteristic feature leading to the unique physical properties of the ionomers.<sup>2–</sup> <sup>6</sup> The multiplets cause the restriction in the mobility of polymer chains surrounding them.<sup>7</sup> As the ion content increases, the restricted mobility regions start to overlap, forming large continuous (i.e., ion-rich) regions that exhibit their own glass-transition temperature $( T _ { \mathrm { g } } ) _ { \mathrm { : } }$called cluster $T _ { \mathrm { g } } \left( \mathrm { i } . \mathrm { e } . , T _ { \mathrm { g 2 } } \right)$, at a much higher temperature than the matrix $T _ { \mathrm { g } } \ : ( \mathrm { i } . \mathrm { e } . , T _ { \mathrm { g 1 } } )$

The modifications of polymer surfaces have been applied to improve the hydrophilicity of polymer surfaces without changing the bulk properties of the polymer significantly. The hydrophilic property is of importance in determining various polymer properties, including wettability, adhesion, colorability, and biocompatibility. Among the modification techniques, the plasma source ion implantation (PSII) method is an effective technique for providing more stable modified surfaces.<sup>8,9</sup> During PSII treatment, a high negative-voltage pulse is applied to the sample stage.

The high voltage accelerates positive ions in the plasma; thus, the positive ions enter the sample. PSII includes both the plasma process and ionbeam process when the pulse is off and on, respectively. Therefore, the PSII treatment generates various functional groups on the sample surface and modifies layers deeply. However, surfacemodified polymers often exhibit time-dependent properties that make the surface-treatment technique less effective.<sup>10,11</sup> This process, called aging or hydrophobic recovery, partially restores the original hydrophobic surface, which is due to the high surface energy of the hydrophilic groups. To decrease the high surface energy, the reorientation of the hydrophilic groups beneath the sample surface (i.e., the rotation and in-diffusion process of functional groups of high hydrophilicity on the surface into bulk) should occur. In addition, the adsorption of hydrocarbons in air on the polymer surface and the out-diffusion process of short hydrophobic chains in bulk toward the surface also induce the hydrophobic recovery.

In this study, we investigated the surface wettability and compositions of $\mathrm { O _ { 2 } } \mathrm { - P S I I }$treated poly-(styrene-co-acrylate) ionomers as a function of time; the incorporation of ionic groups into a polymer leads to more hydrophilic and more stable polymer surface upon PSII treatment because of the presence of ionic groups on the surface and to the restricted mobility of polymer chains, respectively. To characterize the polymer surfaces, we used various characterization techniques. The wetting properties of the ionomer surfaces were measured by contact-angle measurements. The X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) experiments were performed to explain the relationship between the surface-wetting property and the chemical compositions of the ionomer surface and inner layer. These experiments led us to understand the mechanism of hydrophobic recovery of ionomer surfaces.
EXPERIMENTAL
Sample Preparation

Poly(styrene-co-acrylic acid) [P(S-co-AA)] copolymers were prepared by the free-radical bulk copolymerization of purified styrene and acrylic acid monomers with benzoyl peroxide as the initiator. The detailed procedure is described elsewhere.<sup>12</sup> The acid contents of the samples were

2.9, 6.6, 12.2, and 18.9 mol %. To neutralize the acid groups, a predetermined amount of methanolic NaOH and CsOH was added to the P(S-co-AA) samples in a benzene/methanol (9/1 v/v) mixture, which gave Na- and Cs-neutralized poly(styrene-co-acrylate) ionomers—P(S-co-ANa) and P(S-co-ACs)—respectively. The solutions were freeze-dried and then dried further in vacuo at 160 °C for at least 1 day. To make thin polymer films, 7 wt % ionomer–tetrahydrofuran solutions were deposited onto a disposable aluminum dish. The solvent was allowed to evaporate slowly for about 5 days. Subsequently, thin-film samples were dried further in vacuo at room temperature for 12 h.
PSII Apparatus

An in-house built PSII device was used to treat the polymer surface. A detailed description of the apparatus is found elsewhere.<sup>13</sup> To generate the plasma, a 13.56-MHz r.f. power supply and an antenna located inside the chamber were used. The base pressure of the chamber was $1 \times 1 0 ^ { - 5 }$Torr. The $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$plasma was generated at a pressure of 1 mTorr and with an r.f. power of 200 W. The polymer samples were placed on the oil-cooled stage surrounded by the plasma and biased to a high negative potential of -5 kV with a pulse width of 10 $\mu \mathbf { s }$at a pulse repetition of 500 Hz. The PSII treatment time was 1 min.
Instrumental Evaluation

Contact angles of the films were measured by the static sessile drop method with a Rame-Hart 100 contact-angle goniometer (Mount Lakes, NJ). The measurements were made with doubly distilled water and diiodomethane. The surface energies were calculated from the contact-angle values by combining a geometrical mean approach and the Young equation.<sup>14,15</sup> To evaluate the changes in compositions and functional groups on the polymer surface, we used a PHI 5800 XPS with monochromatic Al $\mathrm { K } _ { \alpha }$radiation at a power of 350 W. The electron-emission angles for the XPS study were 15, 45, and 90°. Curve fitting and quantification of the peaks were accomplished with the software supplied by the manufacturer.

elements.text: RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
Wetting Properties: Water Contact Angles and Surface Energies

The wettability of polymer surfaces was determined by measuring the contact angles. Table 1 compares the contact angles of water on the surface of untreated P(S-co-AA), P(S-co-ANa), and $\mathrm { P } ( \mathrm { S } { \cdot } c o { - } \mathrm { A C s } )$samples of different acid/ion contents. Table 1 also includes the surface free energies calculated from the water and diiodomethane contact angles. The contact angles of untreated acid copolymers are almost similar at about $8 5 ^ { \circ }$regardless of acid content and slightly higher than that of polystyrene (PS) homopolymer $( \mathrm { i . e . , }$$7 9 ^ { \circ } ;$see Table 2). In the case of P(S-co-ANa) ionomers, the contact angles for ionomers containing 2.9 and 6.6 mol % of ions are higher than those of acid copolymers. The contact angle of the 12.2 mol % ionomer is, however, lower than that of the acid copolymer. These results indicate that the presence of a small number of ionic groups in the polymer makes the polymer surface more hydrophobic. This can be understood. When the acid groups on the polymer surface, being hydrophilic, become ionic groups by neutralization, the ionic groups interact strongly with other ionic groups, forming multiplets. Naturally, this multiplet formation would occur mainly beneath the polymer surface. However, with increasing ion content some of the hydrophilic ionic groups start to be exposed to air. Thus, the ionomer surface becomes more hydrophilic. In the case of the P(S-co-ACs) ionomers, the water contact angles are lower than those of the P(S-co-ANa) ionomers. This can also be understood. Because the size of the $\mathrm { C s ^ { + } }$ion (radius: 1.74 Å) is much larger than that of the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ion (radius: 1.02 Å),<sup>16</sup> the $\mathrm { { C s } ^ { + } }$ions on the surface may occupy more surface area than the $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ions. In addition, it should also be considered that the entrance of the large $\mathrm { { C s } ^ { + } }$ions beneath the polymer surface is naturally more difficult than that of the small $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$ions.<sup>11</sup>

elements.text: The calculation of surface free energy $( \gamma _ { \mathrm { s } } )$consisting of polar force $( \gamma _ { \mathrm { s } } ^ { \mathrm { p } } )$and dispersive force $( \gamma _ { \mathrm { s } } ^ { \mathrm { d } } )$, with the water and diiodomethane contact-angle data is useful for understanding surface properties.<sup>17,18</sup> In Table 1, the $\gamma _ { \mathrm { s } } \mathrm { ^ { \circ } } \mathbf { s }$for the two ionomer systems increase slightly with an increasing ion content. In addition, the $\gamma _ { \mathrm { s } } ^ { \mathrm { p } }$value increases noticeably with ion content, and the value for the P(S-co-ANa) system is smaller than that for the P(S-co-ACs) system at a comparable ion content. However, in the case of the $\gamma _ { \mathrm { s } } ^ { \mathrm { d } }$value, being much larger than the $\gamma _ { \mathrm { s } } ^ { \mathrm { p } }$value, the value for the P(S-co-ANa) system is larger than that for the P(S-co-ACs) system, and the values do not change significantly with ion content.

Figure 1 shows the plots of water contact angles as a function of aging time for the PSIItreated ionomers of various ion contents. In Figure 1(b), the initial contact angles for the P(S-co-ANa) ionomer are reduced to below $1 0 ^ { \circ }$by PSII treatment, and the P(S-co-ANa) ionomer exhibits very slow hydrophobic recovery behavior. The initial contact angles for the P(S-co-ACs) ionomers are slightly higher than those for the P(S-co-ANa) samples [Fig. 1(c)]; the angles also remain more or less unchanged at low contact angles for 40 days. However, in the case of P(S-co-AA) copolymers [Fig. 1(a)], the contact angle increases gradually with increasing aging time. Also, the ion content does not change the contact-angle values significantly.

The surface free energies for $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 ^ { - } }$PSII treated ionomers are listed in Table 2. The $\gamma _ { \mathrm { s } }$values for the PS homopolymer and acid copolymer containing 6.6 mol % of acid groups, P(S-6.6-AA), initially increase significantly upon PSII treatment and then decrease with aging time. In the case of the 6.6 mol $\%$ionomers, that is, P(S-6.6-ANa) and P(S-6.6-ACs), the PSII treatment increases the $\gamma _ { \mathrm { s } }$values, especially $\gamma _ { \mathrm { s } } ^ { \mathrm { p } }$values, drastically, and the $\gamma _ { \mathrm { s } }$values do not change significantly with aging time.

The strength of ionic interactions in multiplets is one of the useful factors for explaining the results that the modified surfaces of P(S-6.6-ANa) and P(S-6.6-ACs) ionomers are more stable than those of the P(S-6.6-AA) copolymers. As mentioned before,<sup>7</sup> the multiplets restrict the polymer chain mobility, and the hydrophilic functional groups introduced by the PSII treatment and the ionic groups experience difficulties in rotating and hiding inside the polymer sample. The P(S-6.6-ANa) ionomers have a lower hydrophobic recovery than the P(S-6.6-ACs) ionomers. This can be understood. Because the interactions between ionic groups in multiplets are stronger for the P(S-6.6-ANa) ionomers than for the P(S-6.6-ACs) ionomers because of the smaller size of $\mathrm { N a ^ { + } }$as compared with $\mathrm { { C s ^ { + } } }$, the multiplets in the Na ionomer system are more stable than in the Cs ionomers.<sup>4</sup> <sup>–7,19,20</sup> This aspect can be supported by the fact that the $T _ { \mathrm { g 1 } }$and $T _ { \mathrm { g 2 } }$of the P(S-6.6-ANa) ionomer are about 7 and 20 ${ } ^ { \circ } \mathbf { C }$, respectively, higher than those of the P(S-6.6-ACs) ionomer. This implies that the former ionomer needs higher temperature for polymer chain segments to move as compared with the latter ionomer. This difference in chain mobility probably causes the different hydrophobic recovery rates in the two ionomer systems.

elements.text: Surface Compositions: XPS Results

The chemical bonding and compositions of ionomer materials on the surface and in the layer beneath the surface were investigated with XPS. The atomic compositions of the untreated ionomers are illustrated in Figure 2. The ion-composition values ofionomers are slightly smaller than those obtained by a titration method. As expected, the 18.9 mol $\%$ionomers have higher ion and oxygen contents than the 6.6 mol % ionomers. In the figure, the distributions of ions change slightly with an increasing takeoff angle (i.e., with increasing depth). In addition, the data at the takeoff angle at $\mathbf { 1 5 ^ { \circ } }$tell us that the P(S-6.6- ACs) ionomer has more oxygen and ionic units on the surface than P(S-6.6-ANa). This is consistent with the contact-angle result that the unmodified surface of the P(S-6.6-ACs) ionomer is more hydrophilic than that of the P(S-6.6-ANa) ionomer.

Listed in Table 3 are the atomic compositions of PSII-treated P(S-6.6-AA), P(S-6.6-ANa), and P(S-6.6-ACs) samples obtained at the takeoff angle of $4 5 ^ { \circ }$. The noticeable increases in the oxygen and ion contents of P(S-6.6-ANa) and P(S-6.6- ACs) were seen upon PSII treatment. The oxygen content of a PSII-treated P(S-co-AA) copolymer increases drastically and still remains at high values for 20 days, whereas the water contact angle of treated copolymer changes significantly after 20 days (see Table 2). This result illustrates two of the following aspects: First, contact-angle values are closely dependent on the outmost surface layer. Second, the XPS technique at the takeoff angle of 45° is not surface-sensitive enough to reveal the aging behavior of the polymers in detail because the aging is mainly dependent on the outermost surface layer.

The untreated samples showed a typical PS spectrum consisting of C–C, C–H, or unsaturated bonds (at 285.0 eV) and the satellite component (at 291.1 eV) because of $\pi \to \pi ^ { * }$shake-up transitions. The peaks indicating the presence of acid or ionic groups are not observed in the $\mathrm { C _ { 1 S } }$spectrum because the amount of acid or ionic groups in the sample is not large enough to be detected by XPS. However, the peak for the carboxylate bond for the P(S-18.9-AA) copolymer was observed in the $\mathrm { { C _ { 1 S } } }$spectrum (not shown here). In Figure 3(b), the PSII treatment induces the formation of functional groups containing O<sub>O</sub>C<sub>A</sub>O and O<sub>O</sub>C and destruction ofthe aromatic rings. This result, again, indicates that upon PSII treatment more functional groups containing oxygen are generated on the surface, and the surface becomes more hydrophilic.
CONCLUSIONS

The surfaces of PSII-treated P(S-co-AA) acid copolymer and its Na and Cs ionomers were characterized with contact-angle measurements and XPS. The contact-angle results for the untreated surfaces ofthe acid copolymer and Na and Cs ionomers demonstrated different surface free-energy values; this may be due to the different chemical compositions on the surface, depending on the type of ion species used. Upon PSII treatment, the Na and Cs ionomers had more hydrophilic and stable surfaces than the acid copolymers. This indicated that the wetting properties ofthe ionomers were determined by both oxygen-containing groups and ionic groups on the modified surface. In addition, the reduction of reentering of oxygen-containing groups beneath the surface because of the more restricted chain mobility of the ionomers as compared with nonionic polymers also influenced the hydrophobic recovery behavior of the ionomers. The XPS results indicated that the PSII treatment generated oxygen-containing groups on the polymer surface and made the ionic groups appear on the surface.
